messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

As a pharmacist, Yara had always been drawn to the precision and control of her work. But when her 10-year-old son was diagnosed with leukemia, Yara's world began to unravel. She spent countless hours by his side in the hospital, watching as he underwent round after round of grueling treatment. The beeping of machines, the antiseptic smell, and the sterile white walls all blended together into a nightmare that she couldn't wake up from. As her son slowly recovered, Yara found herself struggling to shake off the feelings of weakness and helplessness that had settled over her. She began to believe that there was something fundamentally wrong with her as a person, that she wasn't strong enough to protect her child from harm. This sense of defective self only intensified when she started thinking about why this had happened to her - was it some kind of punishment? Did she somehow deserve it? The more she dwelled on these questions, the more convinced she became that nothing good could ever happen to her again. These negative appraisals began to seep into every aspect of Yara's life. She started avoiding hospitals and ambulances, unable to bear the sight of them without being transported back to those dark days by her son's bedside. Even the sound of sirens in the distance was enough to send her heart racing. She tried hard not to think about the trauma, but it seemed like every noise, every smell, was a trigger waiting to unleash a flood of memories and emotions. As Yara became more withdrawn, she found it increasingly difficult to relax, even when she knew she was safe. Her mind would start racing, jumping from one worst-case scenario to the next, making it impossible for her to fall asleep or stay asleep. The slightest sound - a creaking floorboard, a rustling of leaves - would send her jolting upright, her heart pounding in her chest. The more Yara struggled with these threats, the more she began to believe that she was indeed weak and defective. She felt like she was walking on eggshells, waiting for the next disaster to strike. And so she suppressed her thoughts, trying not to think about the trauma at all - a strategy that only seemed to make things worse. As time went on, Yara's avoidance behaviors began to take a toll on her relationships and work performance. Her colleagues noticed that she was increasingly distant, always seeming preoccupied and on edge. Patients began to complain that she was curt and dismissive, not the warm and caring pharmacist they had come to trust. And yet, despite these consequences, Yara couldn't seem to break free from the cycle of negative appraisals, threat monitoring, and maladaptive strategies that had taken hold. It wasn't until her son's latest check-up - a routine visit that sent Yara into a tailspin of anxiety - that she realized she needed help. She was exhausted, trapped in a never-ending loop of fear and self-doubt. As she sat in the waiting room, watching as families laughed and chatted together, Yara felt a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, there was a way out of this darkness - a way to break free from the grip of PTSD and start rebuilding her life. Yara's eyes filled with tears as she thought about what had brought her to this point. She was scared - scared that she would never be able to escape the memories of her son's illness, scared that she would never be able to find peace again. But most of all, she was scared that she would lose herself completely in the process. As she stood up, smoothing out her clothes and taking a deep breath, Yara knew that it was time to face her fears head-on - no matter how daunting the journey ahead might seem.
